summary.text: A wind wave is a surface wave raised on a body of water by wind blowing across it, ranging from small ripples to waves over 30 m high.
Their size is limited by wind speed, how long the wind blows, the fetch (the distance it blows over the water) and the water depth.
Once they leave the windy area they become swells that can travel thousands of kilometres, like waves from south of Tasmania that reach southern California.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: From small ripples to over 30 m

facts.label: Significant wave height
facts.value: Average of the highest third of waves

facts.label: Restoring force
facts.value: Surface tension for ripples, gravity for sea waves

items.prompt: A light breeze blows more slowly than the crests of the waves already on the sea. Will it make those waves grow?

options.label: No, wind must outpace the crests to pass them energy
Yes, any wind adds energy to waves it touches
Yes, but only if it blows for a whole day
No, because breezes only affect deep water

items.explain: For energy to transfer to the wave, the wind must be moving faster than the wave crest.

items.prompt: A forecast gives a significant wave height of 4 m for today. What is the largest single wave you should likely expect?

options.label: Exactly 4 m, since that is the forecast
Under 4 m, since the figure is an average
Somewhat less than 8 m
Around 20 m or more

items.explain: Because wave heights vary, the largest waves are likely somewhat less than twice the significant wave height.

items.prompt: The wind suddenly stops. What happens to ripples on a glassy pond and to large sea waves?

options.label: Both vanish within a few seconds
Ripples die quickly; sea waves keep going much longer
Sea waves stop at once; ripples last for hours
Both keep going for days unchanged

items.explain: Ripples, held by surface tension, die quickly when wind stops, while gravity-driven sea waves last much longer.

items.prompt: On a calm, windless day, surfers in southern California find big waves rolling in. Where did those waves most likely come from?

options.label: An underwater earthquake just offshore
The daily pull of the Moon on the coast
Ships passing close to the beach
Swells from storms thousands of kilometres away

items.explain: Swells leave the windy area that made them and travel thousands of kilometres, such as from south of Tasmania to southern California.

items.prompt: An old saying claims the seventh wave in a set is always the biggest. What is actually true?

options.label: The first wave of a set is always the biggest
Middle waves tend to be bigger, but not always the seventh
The seventh wave is always the biggest one
Every wave in a set is the same height

items.explain: The seventh wave is not always largest, but waves in the middle of a set tend to be larger than those before and after.

items.prompt: A steady wind has already built a fully developed sea. It keeps blowing at the same strength for another day. What happens to the waves?

options.label: They keep growing taller without limit
They shrink back to small ripples
They turn into a tsunami
They stop growing; extra energy goes into whitecaps

items.explain: A fully developed sea is the maximum for that wind; more exposure only dissipates energy as wave tops break into whitecaps.
